title: Docker Images: Layers, Cache, and Lean Builds
summary: A dense field guide to how Docker images are actually built and stored — union filesystem layers, content-addressable digests, the build cache and what invalidates it, multi-stage builds, image size reduction, and .dockerignore. Covers mechanics, practical Dockerfile patterns, base-image trade-offs, and the common mistakes that produce 2GB images and cache misses on every build.

chapters.title: What an Image Actually Is
points: Image = ordered stack of read-only filesystem layers + a JSON config (env, entrypoint, cmd, workdir, user) + a manifest tying them together
Layer = a tar archive of filesystem *changes* (added, modified, deleted files) relative to the layer below — not a full filesystem snapshot
Union filesystem (overlay2 on modern Linux) merges layers into one view: upper layers shadow lower ones for same-path files
Container = image layers + one thin writable container layer on top; deleting the container discards only that writable layer
Copy-on-write: modifying a file in a container copies the whole file up into the writable layer first — big file, big copy, even for a one-byte edit
Whiteout files: deleting a file from a lower layer writes a `.wh.<name>` marker in the upper layer; the bytes stay in the image forever
Content addressing: each layer identified by sha256 digest of its content, so identical layers are stored once and shared across images
Image ID is the digest of the *config* JSON; the RepoDigest (`image@sha256:...`) is the digest of the manifest as pushed to a registry
Tags are mutable pointers (`node:20` today ≠ `node:20` next week); digests are immutable — pin digests for reproducibility
`docker image inspect nginx --format '{{json .RootFS.Layers}}'` lists the layer digests; `docker history nginx` shows size per layer

chapters.title: How the Dockerfile Builds Layers
points: One instruction that changes the filesystem = one layer: RUN, COPY, ADD create layers; ENV, LABEL, EXPOSE, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, WORKDIR, USER, ARG only mutate config metadata (zero-byte layers)
FROM sets the parent layer stack; `FROM scratch` starts from an empty filesystem with no layers at all
Each instruction executes against the result of the previous one, so ordering is semantic, not cosmetic
Every RUN runs in a fresh temporary container from the previous layer; shell state does not persist — `RUN cd /app` then `RUN make` runs make in `/`
Use `WORKDIR /app` (persisted in config) instead of `RUN cd /app`; chain dependent shell commands with `&&` in a single RUN
COPY takes files from the build context; ADD additionally auto-extracts local tarballs and can fetch URLs — prefer COPY unless you specifically want extraction
`COPY --chown=app:app` and `COPY --chmod=0755` set ownership/permissions without an extra RUN chmod layer (which would duplicate every touched file)
Layer count itself is cheap (no meaningful runtime cost; the old 127-layer limit is effectively gone) — layer *content* is what costs bytes
Build context is tarred and shipped to the daemon before the build starts; a 3GB context means a 3GB upload even if you COPY one file
BuildKit (default in modern Docker) builds a DAG and can run independent stages in parallel and skip stages nothing depends on
Example anti-layer: `RUN apt-get update` in one layer and `RUN apt-get install -y curl` in the next — the cached update layer goes stale and you install from an old package index

layout.note: Ch 2: How the Dockerfile Builds Layers
Instruction | Creates layer? | Notes — FROM(base stack) / RUN(yes) / COPY(yes) / ADD(yes, auto-extract) / ENV,LABEL,WORKDIR,USER,CMD,ENTRYPOINT,EXPOSE,ARG(metadata only)
Bad vs good: RUN cd /app + RUN make  ✗   vs   WORKDIR /app + RUN make  ✓ ; and split apt-get update/install vs chained &&
Each RUN is a fresh container; no shell state persists; COPY --chown/--chmod avoids a duplicating chmod layer
Build context: whole directory tarred and sent to daemon first — context size is upload cost, separate from image size
Layer count is cheap. Layer bytes are not. Optimize content, not the number of instructions.

chapters.title: The Build Cache: How It Decides to Reuse
points: Cache is keyed per instruction on (parent layer digest + the instruction's cache key); a miss on one step invalidates every step after it
For RUN, the cache key is the literal command string — Docker does not know or check what the command actually does
For COPY/ADD, the cache key includes a checksum of the copied file contents plus metadata (mode, ownership) — content changes bust it, mtime alone does not
Consequence: `RUN apt-get install -y curl` stays cached forever even though upstream package versions moved on — cache hits can mean stale software
Consequence: change one line of app source and every layer after `COPY . .` rebuilds
Golden ordering rule: least-frequently-changing steps first, most-frequently-changing (your source code) last
Dependency-manifest split: `COPY package*.json ./` then `RUN npm ci` then `COPY . .` — source edits skip the dependency install entirely
Same pattern per ecosystem: requirements.txt / poetry.lock (pip), go.mod+go.sum (go mod download), Cargo.toml+Cargo.lock (cargo fetch), pom.xml (mvn dependency:go-offline)
`--no-cache` rebuilds everything; `--pull` re-fetches the base image so a moved tag is actually picked up
ARG values participate in the cache key from the point of use — a changing ARG (like a build timestamp or git SHA) placed early nukes the whole cache; declare it just before it is needed
BuildKit cache mounts persist a package cache *across* builds without shipping it in the image: `RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci`
CI has no local cache by default — use `--cache-from` with a registry image, or BuildKit `--cache-to type=registry,mode=max` to export intermediate layers

layout.note: Ch 3: The Build Cache — How It Decides to Reuse
Cache key = parent layer + instruction key; one miss invalidates the entire tail of the Dockerfile.
Instruction | Cache key basis — RUN: literal command text / COPY,ADD: content checksum + mode + owner / ENV,ARG: value at point of use
Cache-friendly Node ordering: FROM node:20-alpine / WORKDIR /app / COPY package*.json ./ / RUN npm ci / COPY . . / CMD
Two vertical Dockerfile columns side by side, cached steps green and rebuilt steps red, showing COPY . . placed early (all red below) vs placed last (only last step red)
BuildKit cache mount: RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci — cache persists between builds, ships zero bytes
Cache hit can mean stale: RUN apt-get install never re-resolves versions. Use --no-cache --pull for periodic rebuilds.

chapters.title: Multi-Stage Builds
points: Syntax: multiple FROM instructions in one Dockerfile; each FROM starts a new stage with its own layer stack
Name stages with `FROM golang:1.22 AS builder`, then pull artifacts across with `COPY --from=builder /src/app /usr/local/bin/app`
Only the final stage's layers ship — compilers, headers, build caches, and source in earlier stages are discarded entirely
This solves the classic problem that `RUN make && rm -rf /build-deps` cannot shrink the image, because the deps still exist in an earlier layer
Go example: builder stage `RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /app`, final stage `FROM scratch` + `COPY --from=builder /app /app` — resulting image is a single static binary, a few MB
Node example: builder runs `npm ci && npm run build`, runtime stage runs `npm ci --omit=dev` and copies only `dist/` and production `node_modules`
`COPY --from=nginx:alpine /etc/nginx/nginx.conf ./` — you can copy from an external image, not just from your own stages
`--target=builder` builds only up to a named stage: useful for a test stage in CI or for debugging a build that fails at the copy step
BuildKit builds only the stages the final target depends on, and builds independent stages in parallel
Common stage layout: `base` (shared setup) → `deps` → `builder` → `test` → `runtime`, with test depending on builder but runtime not depending on test
Gotcha: `COPY --from` copies file contents only — it does not carry over ENV, WORKDIR, USER, or installed system packages from that stage

Gotcha: a dynamically linked binary copied into `scratch` or `distroless` fails with 'no such file or directory' (the missing thing is the loader/libc, not your binary) — build static or use a matching runtime base

layout.note: Ch 4: Multi-Stage Builds

Two boxes: left 'builder' stage (large, contains toolchain+source+object files) with a single arrow labelled COPY --from=builder carrying one small artifact into a tiny right box 'runtime'; discarded builder shown greyed out

Full Go multi-stage: FROM golang:1.22 AS builder / WORKDIR /src / COPY go.mod go.sum ./ / RUN go mod download / COPY . . / RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /app  ||  FROM gcr.io/distroless/static / COPY --from=builder /app /app / ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
Named stages; copy from external images; --target for test/debug stages; parallel independent stages; deps/builder/test/runtime layout
Why rm -rf can't shrink an image: earlier layer still holds the bytes; only a new stage truly drops them
COPY --from moves files, not environment. Static-link or match the runtime base, or scratch gives you 'no such file or directory'.

chapters.title: .dockerignore and the Build Context
points: Before any instruction runs, the CLI packs the build context directory into a tar and sends it to the daemon — `.dockerignore` filters what goes into that tar
File lives at the root of the build context, not necessarily next to the Dockerfile; BuildKit also honors `<dockerfile-name>.dockerignore`
Syntax is Go filepath.Match-based, not gitignore: `*` does not cross `/`, `**` matches any depth, `#` starts a comment
`!pattern` re-includes something an earlier pattern excluded; order matters and the last matching rule wins
Patterns are relative to the context root — `node_modules` matches only the top level, `**/node_modules` matches everywhere
Three separate wins: smaller/faster context upload, fewer accidental cache busts from `COPY . .`, and no secrets or junk baked into the image
Cache impact is the sharp edge: without `.dockerignore`, touching `.git/` or a local log file changes the COPY checksum and rebuilds everything after it

Security: `.env`, `.git` (full history and any leaked past secrets), `*.pem`, `id_rsa`, `.aws/`, `.npmrc` with tokens must be excluded — `COPY . .` copies them into a layer anyone who pulls can extract

Standard starter set: `.git`, `node_modules`, `dist`, `build`, `target`, `__pycache__`, `*.pyc`, `.venv`, `.env*`, `*.log`, `.DS_Store`, `coverage`, `.pytest_cache`, `Dockerfile`, `.dockerignore`, `README.md`
Note the inversion trick for strictness: `*` then `!src/` `!package.json` — allowlist instead of denylist, so new junk directories are excluded by default
Verify with `docker build --progress=plain .` and read the 'transferring context' size, or `du -sh` the directory minus your ignores

Common mistake: ignoring `node_modules` but relying on it being copied in — you must `RUN npm ci` inside the image instead (which is what you wanted anyway, since host-built native modules are the wrong architecture)

layout.note: Ch 5: .dockerignore and the Build Context
Left: project dir with .git, node_modules, .env, src greyed out by a filter labelled .dockerignore; arrow 'context tar → daemon' carrying only src + manifests
Sample .dockerignore with comments: .git / **/node_modules / *.log / .env* / dist / plus the allowlist inversion: * then !src !package.json !package-lock.json
Pattern | Matches — node_modules(top level only) / **/node_modules(any depth) / *.log(top-level logs) / !keep.log(re-include)
Three wins: upload size, cache stability, secret hygiene
COPY . . with no .dockerignore ships .git and .env into a layer. Anyone who pulls the image can read them — deleting later does not help.

chapters.title: Shrinking Image Size
points: Measure first: `docker images` for totals, `docker history --no-trunc ` for per-layer size, and `dive ` to see wasted bytes and per-layer file diffs
Base image choice dominates: debian ~120MB, ubuntu ~78MB, alpine ~7MB, distroless static ~2MB, scratch 0MB — pick the smallest that runs your binary
`-slim` variants (e.g. `python:3.12-slim`) drop docs, man pages, and dev tooling while keeping glibc — usually the best default when alpine's musl is a problem
Clean inside the same RUN, never after: `RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*` — the rm in a later RUN would not shrink anything
`--no-install-recommends` (apt), `--no-cache` (apk), `--no-cache-dir` (pip), `npm ci --omit=dev`, `go clean -modcache` — per-tool ways to avoid caching package archives into the layer
Multi-stage is the single biggest lever for compiled languages: ship the artifact, drop the toolchain
Strip binaries (`go build -ldflags="-s -w"`, `strip`) and disable CGO for static Go builds
Do not chase size by cramming everything into one giant RUN — you destroy cache granularity; balance layer reuse against total bytes
Squashing / `--squash` collapses layers into one: smaller image, but every rebuild transfers the whole thing and cross-image layer sharing is lost
Registry pull cost is what actually matters to users: shared base layers are downloaded once, so 5 images on one base cost far less than the sum of their sizes
Multi-arch note: `--platform` mismatches silently pull an emulated image; build with buildx for the target arch rather than shipping a fat wrong-arch image
Worked comparison: naive Node image `FROM node:20` + `COPY . .` + `npm install` ≈ 1.1GB → alpine base + dependency-split + multi-stage + prod-only deps ≈ 150MB

layout.note: Ch 6: Shrinking Image Size
Base | Approx size | Use when — scratch 0MB(static binary) / distroless ~2MB(no shell, prod) / alpine ~7MB(musl OK) / debian-slim ~75MB(glibc needed) / debian ~120MB(full tooling)
apt cleanup in one RUN: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
Measure with docker history / dive; per-tool no-cache flags; strip binaries; multi-stage for compiled langs
Squash trade-off: one layer = smaller image, but full re-transfer per rebuild and no shared base layers
Before/after bar chart: 1.1GB naive node image vs 150MB optimized, annotated with which technique removed which chunk
rm -rf in a later RUN removes nothing from the image. Clean in the same RUN that created the mess.

chapters.title: Alpine vs Slim vs Distroless vs Scratch
points: Alpine uses musl libc and BusyBox, not glibc and GNU coreutils — most incompatibilities trace back to that one fact
Python on alpine is the classic trap: manylinux wheels are glibc-only, so pip compiles C extensions from source — builds get 5-10x slower and the image ends up *larger* than slim after pulling in gcc

Known musl issues: different DNS resolver behavior (historically no `search` domain / TCP fallback edge cases), smaller default thread stack size causing stack overflows in some runtimes, and past malloc performance gaps under heavy multithreading
Debian `-slim`: glibc, apt available, prebuilt wheels work, ~75MB — the boring correct default for Python/Ruby/Node when you are unsure
Distroless (`gcr.io/distroless/*`): only your app plus its runtime deps and CA certs — no shell, no package manager, no busybox
No shell means `docker exec -it ... sh` fails and `RUN` cannot be used in that stage — distroless is a runtime-stage-only base, and you debug with the `:debug` variant or `docker debug`
Distroless security win: no shell to exploit, tiny package surface, so almost nothing for a CVE scanner to flag

Scratch: literally empty. Works only for fully static binaries (Go with CGO_ENABLED=0, Rust musl target). You must add CA certs yourself (`COPY --from=builder /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt`) or every HTTPS call fails
Scratch also has no `/etc/passwd`, no `/tmp`, and no timezone database — set `USER 65532:65532` numerically and copy in `/usr/share/zoneinfo` if your app needs local time
Decision rule: static compiled binary → scratch/distroless-static; JVM/Node/Python needing glibc → distroless-java/nodejs or debian-slim; need a shell in production for ops → alpine or slim
Size is not the only axis — compare on build time, CVE surface, debuggability, and ecosystem compatibility together
Everything here applies to the *final* stage; the builder stage should use the full fat image with the whole toolchain

layout.note: Ch 7: Alpine vs Slim vs Distroless vs Scratch

Base | libc | Shell | Pkg mgr | Size | Best for — alpine(musl/busybox sh/apk/~7MB/small ops-friendly) / debian-slim(glibc/bash/apt/~75MB/Python,Node default) / distroless(glibc/none/none/~2-50MB/prod runtime) / scratch(none/none/none/0MB/static binaries)
The alpine trap explained: musl + no manylinux wheels = source compiles, slow builds, sometimes a bigger image than slim.
Scratch CA certs + nonroot: COPY --from=builder /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt /etc/ssl/certs/ / USER 65532:65532
Q: Why does docker exec fail on my distroless image? A: There is no shell in it — use the :debug variant or docker debug.
Optimize the final stage only. The builder stage should be fat and full of tools.

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Anti-Patterns
points: `COPY . .` before installing dependencies — every source edit reinstalls the whole dependency tree; split the manifest copy out
`RUN apt-get update` and `RUN apt-get install` in separate layers — the cached update goes stale and you install against an old index
`rm -rf /tmp/build` in a RUN after the one that created it — bytes stay in the earlier layer, image size unchanged; clean in-place or use a stage
Secrets via ARG or ENV: `ARG NPM_TOKEN` is visible in `docker history` and any ENV persists into the running container — use `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc` instead, which never lands in a layer
`ADD https://...` for downloads — no checksum verification, silently busts cache differently than expected; use `RUN curl -fsSL ... && echo "<sha> file" | sha256sum -c`
`FROM node:latest` or any floating tag — non-reproducible builds and surprise major-version breakage; pin to `node:20.11.1-alpine` or a digest
Running as root: default USER is root, so a container escape starts with root; add `RUN adduser --system app` and `USER app` (or a numeric UID for scratch/distroless)
Installing debug tools (curl, vim, netcat, build-essential) in the production stage 'just in case' — that is size *and* attack surface
No `.dockerignore` at all — huge context upload, constant cache busts, and secrets copied into layers
Using `latest` cache from CI without `--pull` — the base image tag moved upstream and you never get the security patch
One giant RUN with everything chained — great for size, terrible for cache; you rebuild the entire toolchain on any change
Forgetting `.git` in the context: it drags in full history (often hundreds of MB) and changes on every commit, so it busts the cache on literally every build

layout.note: Ch 8: Common Mistakes and Anti-Patterns

Anti-pattern | Why it hurts | Fix — COPY . . first(rebuilds deps/split manifest) / split apt update(stale index/chain &&) / rm in later RUN(no size win/same RUN or stage) / ARG secret(in docker history/--mount=type=secret) / FROM latest(non-reproducible/pin digest)
Secret done right: RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci   vs   ARG NPM_TOKEN ✗ visible in docker history
Root by default; debug tools in prod stage; missing .dockerignore; no --pull in CI; one mega-RUN kills cache
docker history shows every build arg and command. Anything you passed as ARG is readable by anyone with the image.

chapters.title: Practical Recipes and Cheat Sheet
points: Node production Dockerfile: builder stage `npm ci` + `npm run build`; runtime stage `npm ci --omit=dev`, `COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist`, `USER node`, `CMD ["node","dist/main.js"]`

Python production Dockerfile: `python:3.12-slim`, builder installs into a venv at `/opt/venv` with `pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt`, runtime copies the venv and sets `ENV PATH=/opt/venv/bin:$PATH`
Go production Dockerfile: `go mod download` before `COPY . .`, `CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -ldflags="-s -w"`, final stage `gcr.io/distroless/static:nonroot`
Always exec-form CMD/ENTRYPOINT (`CMD ["node","app.js"]`) — shell form wraps in `/bin/sh -c`, which swallows SIGTERM and breaks graceful shutdown
Add `HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s CMD [...]` and a `LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source=<repo>` for registry linkage
Debug commands: `docker history --no-trunc`, `dive`, `docker build --progress=plain --no-cache`, `docker run --rm -it <builder-stage-id> sh` to poke at an intermediate stage
`docker builder prune` reclaims cache disk; `docker system df` shows what layers and build cache are costing you locally
CI caching: `docker buildx build --cache-from type=registry,ref=repo/app:cache --cache-to type=registry,ref=repo/app:cache,mode=max` (mode=max exports intermediate stages too)
Rebuild cadence: weekly `--no-cache --pull` scheduled build so base-image security patches actually land, even when every layer would otherwise cache-hit
Reproducibility: pin base by digest, commit your lockfile, and use `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` / buildx `--build-arg BUILDKIT_INLINE_CACHE=1` where determinism matters
Summary rules: order by change frequency, split manifests from source, clean in the same RUN, ship only artifacts via multi-stage, ignore aggressively, pin bases, never run as root
Final mental model: an image is a cache-friendly stack of diffs — you optimize it by controlling what changes, how often, and at which layer
